paragraphs.heading: Who Galileo was
paragraphs.text: Galileo Galilei lived from 1564 to 1642 and is often called simply Galileo. He was an Italian astronomer, physicist and engineer, and a polymath. He was born in Pisa, which then belonged to the Duchy of Florence. He has been named the father of observational astronomy, of classical physics, of the scientific method and of modern science.

paragraphs.heading: The swinging chandelier
paragraphs.text: His father pushed him toward medicine, so in 1580 he enrolled at the University of Pisa, though he had seriously thought about becoming a priest. In 1581, while still a medical student, he watched a chandelier swinging in moving air, sometimes in wide arcs and sometimes in narrow ones. Timing it against his own heartbeat, he thought each swing took the same time whatever its size. At home he hung two pendulums of equal length, set one swinging widely and the other only a little, and saw that they stayed in step.

paragraphs.heading: A mind for motion and machines
paragraphs.text: Galileo studied speed and velocity, gravity and free fall, inertia, projectile motion and the principle of relativity. He also turned to practical science, describing how pendulums and "hydrostatic balances" behave. He was among the earliest makers of the thermoscope, invented several kinds of military compass, and built an early microscope.

paragraphs.heading: What the telescope showed
paragraphs.text: Galileo built an improved telescope. Through it he saw the phases of Venus, the stars that make up the Milky Way, the four biggest moons of Jupiter, the rings of Saturn, craters on the Moon and spots on the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: Collision with the Church
paragraphs.text: Galileo openly backed Copernican heliocentrism, the system of Copernicus, and this drew opposition from inside the Catholic Church and from some astronomers. In 1615 the Roman Inquisition looked into the matter and decided his views went against accepted readings of the Bible. In 1632 he defended his views in his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems. The book seemed to argue with and mock Pope Urban VIII, and it turned both the Pope and the Jesuits against him, although both had strongly supported him until then.

paragraphs.heading: Trial and house arrest
paragraphs.text: The Inquisition put Galileo on trial, judged him "vehemently suspect of heresy", and made him take back his views. He lived under house arrest for the rest of his life. Even so, he kept working: in 1638 he published Two New Sciences, a book mainly about kinematics and the strength of materials.

paragraphs.heading: A musical family
paragraphs.text: His father, Vincenzo Galilei, was a leading lute player, composer and music theorist, and Galileo became a skilled lutenist too. Galileo was the eldest of six children. With Marina Gamba, outside marriage, he had two daughters and a son. Both daughters became nuns for life at the convent of San Matteo in Arcetri, where the elder, Virginia, took the name Maria Celeste.
